data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":{"adopted_commitment_refs":[],"disanalogies":["Design by Contract typically targets object-level preconditions and postconditions, while the problem concerns a set-level invariant over dynamically growing committed evidence.","Contract-based testing is usually framed around method-call semantics, whereas the artifact-count problem concerns metadata and repository structure."],"overturn_conditions":["If published testing principles directly endorse exact-count assertions for committed artifacts as a correctness criterion, the proposed universal invariant is overturned.","If the source materials do not actually articulate a per-element invariant principle, the transfer claim from Design by Contract is unsupported.","If a stronger published principle explicitly mandates cardinality-sensitive tests for committed evidence, the proposed property is insufficient."],"shared_structure":["Both the regression test problem and Design by Contract distinguish between behavioral properties (per-element contract) and incidental structural counts (set size).","Both involve invariant preservation under expected system evolution: contracts remain valid across compliant changes.","Both separate stable correctness criteria from fragile implementation coupling."],"source_memory_refs":["SRC_001","SRC_002"],"transfer_claims":["The principle that tests should verify behavioral contracts rather than exact implementation states transfers to the artifact-count problem: test per-artifact compliance rather than exact cardinality.","The Open-Closed reasoning supporting behavioral contract preservation supports the claim that the regression test should be open to compliant extension."]},"claim":"A regression test that pins an exact artifact count is brittle; it should instead assert a universal invariance over every element of the committed set. The property to assert is a per-artifact contract holding for every committed item, supporting an invariant that remains valid when new compliant evidence is added.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If the problem specifically requires an exact-count semantic invariant, asserting only a per-element universal property would fail to detect cardinality regressions.","eval":"observation"},{"case":"If no per-artifact contract can be formulated for the committed set, the universal invariance approach fails to yield a concrete test.","eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the committed set is intentionally closed and extension is a defect, then testing for openness is undesirable and the proposed invariant is wrong.","eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"By quantifying universally over committed artifacts rather than over the cardinality of the set, the test expresses a property preserved under set extension. This is the published testing principle of invariant preservation over structural growth: tests should verify that each element of the set satisfies a contract, not that the set has a particular size. This aligns with Design by Contract, where preconditions and postconditions are stated over object behavior rather than over incidental counts.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
